newsitem.title: CHINA: New HK chamber wastes little time in passing laws.
newsitem.headline: New HK chamber wastes little time in passing laws.

text.p: Hours after it was sworn in on Tuesday, Hong Kong's new Beijing-anointed legislature passed an omnibus bill activating laws curbing protests and the funding of political parties.
The bill covered legislation that the 60-member assembly had adopted ahead of the return of the territory to communist China at midnight on Monday after 156 years of colonial rule.
The nine-part Hong Kong Reunification Bill, adopted by voice vote, also endorsed the appointments of top judges of the Special Administrative Region (SAR) and the establishment of its legal system.
Britain's Prince Charles handed back the territory to Chinese President Jiang Zemin in a gala ceremony at Hong Kong's Convention Centre.
Post-handover leader Tung Chee-hwa, his administration and the provisional legislature were sworn in a few hours later.
The new chamber was meeting for the first time on Hong Kong soil after holding sessions across the border in the Chinese city of Shenzhen to stave off challenges by the territory's democrats.

The pro-democracy camp, which has strongly criticised curbs on political reforms, had said it would be illegal for the lawmakers to meet in Hong Kong as long as the partially-elected legislative council continued to sit in the territory.
The legislative council ceased to exist at midnight.
Rita Fan, the chamber's president, told legislators they needed to pass an electoral law so that elections for a new legislature could be held as soon as possible.
Tung has pledged that the elections would be held next May.
Of 20 lawmakers who stood up to speak on the omnibus bill, 19 were in favour.

Lawmaker Frederick Fung, who was also a member of the dissolved legislature, said he had "reservations" about amendments to laws on societies and public order. Fung said he was "cautiously optimistic" about the "one country, two systems" policy devised by China's late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping to allow capitalist Hong Kong to co-exist with the communist mainland.
China's and Hong Kong's financial investment could support each other, creating a win-win situation, he said.
